adjudication_records.issue_text: app/controllers/embed_controller.rb:15 — Every miss enqueues a job before throttling, so repeated or query-varied requests from the allowed host can flood the queue and outbound fetches.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the embed_controller.rb code at line 15, when topic_id is nil, it enqueues a job with `Jobs.enqueue(:retrieve_topic, ...)`. The throttling logic is in TopicRetriever (lib/topic_retriever.rb), specifically in the `retrieved_recently?` method which uses Redis to throttle to once every 60 seconds per embed_url. However, the job is enqueued BEFORE any throttling check happens - the throttling only occurs inside the job's `retrieve` method. This means every request to the embed endpoint with a new/unknown embed_url will enqueue a job, and the throttling only prevents the actual HTTP fetch, not the job creation. Additionally, different query parameters on the same URL would create different embed_urls, potentially bypassing the throttle. The finding is correct that repeated requests can flood the job queue since the enqueue happens unconditionally before throttling.

adjudication_records.issue_text: lib/topic_retriever.rb:49 — A configured embeddable host with a blank embed_by_username crashes every retrieval job on downcase and leaves embeds permanently loading.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at lib/topic_retriever.rb:49, the code is `user = User.where(username_lower: SiteSetting.embed_by_username.downcase).first`. If embed_by_username is blank (empty string), calling .downcase on it returns an empty string, which won't crash - it will just return nil for user. The next line `return if user.blank?` handles this case gracefully. However, the finding claims this 'crashes every retrieval job on downcase' - this is incorrect. An empty string.downcase returns an empty string, not an error. The code handles the blank user case by returning early. The finding is not accurate about the crash behavior.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/models/topic_embed.rb:48 — The allowed host is checked only before open follows redirects, so an allowed URL can redirect the worker to an internal or otherwise forbidden destination.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the code in app/models/topic_embed.rb:48, the import_remote method uses `open(url).read` to fetch content from a URL. The method does check that the URL matches the embeddable_host setting in topic_retriever.rb's invalid_host? method before calling perform_retrieve, which eventually calls fetch_http -> TopicEmbed.import_remote. However, the finding points out that `open()` (from open-uri) follows HTTP redirects by default. So if an attacker controls content at an allowed host (e.g., eviltrout.com), they could set up a redirect to an internal service (like http://localhost:6379 for Redis, or internal AWS metadata endpoints). The host validation happens before the HTTP request, but the actual request via `open()` will follow redirects to any destination. This is a valid Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) vulnerability - the allowed URL can redirect to forbidden/internal destinations.

adjudication_records.issue_text: lib/topic_retriever.rb:41 — Any feed fetch or parse failure aborts retrieval before the direct HTTP fallback, coupling one broken feed to every uncached embed.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at lib/topic_retriever.rb:41, the perform_retrieve method calls Jobs::PollFeed.new.execute({}) when feed_polling_enabled? is true. In lib/jobs/scheduled/poll_feed.rb, the poll_feed method uses SimpleRSS.parse(open(SiteSetting.feed_polling_url)) which can throw exceptions on network failures or parse errors. If this throws an exception, the perform_retrieve method would abort before reaching the fetch_http fallback on line 49. This is a real bug - any RSS feed failure would prevent the direct HTTP fetch from being attempted for that embed URL.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/jobs/scheduled/poll_feed.rb:35 — One feed item with missing or invalid content aborts all later items while retries are disabled, silently leaving the remainder stale for an hour.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at app/jobs/scheduled/poll_feed.rb lines 30-36, the code iterates over rss.items with `rss.items.each do |i|`. If any item has missing content (i.content is nil), calling `.scrub` on nil would raise NoMethodError. Additionally, if CGI.unescapeHTML receives invalid input or TopicEmbed.import raises an exception, the entire loop would abort. Since `sidekiq_options retry: false` is set on line 12, failed jobs won't retry, and the scheduler runs hourly. This means one bad feed item could prevent all subsequent items from being processed for an hour. This is a real robustness issue - the code lacks error handling around individual item processing.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/models/topic_embed.rb:48 — Remote reads have no explicit connection or read timeout, allowing a slow source to pin background workers indefinitely.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at app/models/topic_embed.rb:48, the code uses `open(url).read` from the open-uri library without specifying any timeout options. This is in the `import_remote` method which fetches content from external URLs. The open-uri library by default has no timeout, meaning a slow or malicious server could keep the connection open indefinitely, blocking the worker thread. This is a real issue - background jobs (like RetrieveTopic) call this method, and without timeouts, a slow external source could pin workers indefinitely. The same issue exists in app/jobs/scheduled/poll_feed.rb:27 with `open(SiteSetting.feed_polling_url)`. This is a legitimate operational/reliability concern.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/assets/javascripts/embed.js:17 — Substring-based origin validation accepts shorter attacker-controlled origins that prefix discourseUrl and lets them send arbitrary resize messages.
matched_golden_ids: The current origin validation using indexOf is insufficient and can be bypassed. An attacker could use a malicious domain like evil-discourseUrl.com to pass this check.
adjudication_records.primary_judge_reasoning: Both comments identify the same security vulnerability: the origin validation using indexOf/substring matching is insufficient and can be bypassed. The golden comment mentions an attacker using 'evil-discourseUrl.com' while the candidate mentions 'attacker-controlled origins that prefix discourseUrl'. Both are describing the same bypass technique where a malicious domain containing the legitimate domain as a substring can pass the validation check.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/models/topic_embed.rb:36 — Post revision and content_sha1 advancement are not atomic and the revise result is ignored, so a failed revision can mark stale content as current.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the code in app/models/topic_embed.rb around line 36, I see the update logic: `revisor.revise!(user, absolutize_urls(url, contents), skip_validations: true, bypass_rate_limiter: true)` followed by `embed.update_column(:content_sha1, content_sha1)`. The finding claims these are not atomic and the revise result is ignored. This is accurate - if `revise!` fails (returns false), the code still proceeds to update the content_sha1 via `update_column`. This means if the revision fails for any reason, the embed record will be marked with the new content_sha1 even though the post wasn't actually updated, causing the system to think the content is current when it's actually stale. This is a real bug - the return value of `revise!` should be checked before updating the content_sha1.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/controllers/embed_controller.rb:9 — The embed endpoint never verifies that embed_url belongs to the authorized referrer host, so invalid requests receive a perpetually reloading loading page instead of a validation error.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the embed_controller.rb, the ensure_embeddable method validates that request.referer host matches SiteSetting.embeddable_host. However, the embed_url parameter passed to the best action is not validated against the embeddable_host. The code in topic_retriever.rb does check that the embed_url host matches embeddable_host in the invalid_host? method, but this happens asynchronously in the job. In the controller's best action, if topic_id is nil, it enqueues a job and renders 'loading' without validating embed_url. The loading page has a 30-second auto-refresh. If someone passes an embed_url with a different host than embeddable_host, the TopicRetriever will reject it (invalid_host? returns true), but the controller will keep showing the loading page that refreshes every 30 seconds. This is indeed a real issue - invalid embed_urls result in an infinite loading loop rather than a proper error.

adjudication_records.issue_text: lib/tasks/disqus.thor:117 — Removing the public --category/-c option breaks existing Disqus import invocations and silently drops their category-selection capability without a deprecation path.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the diff for lib/tasks/disqus.thor, the method_option for --category/-c is removed at line 117, and the code that used category_id is also removed (lines 144-147 in the original). This means existing users who were using the --category option in their Disqus import commands will now have that option silently ignored or cause an error, and their topics will no longer be placed in the specified category. This is a breaking change to a public CLI interface without any deprecation warning or migration path.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/jobs/scheduled/poll_feed.rb:35 — RSS items without a content field raise on nil.scrub and abort the entire poll instead of importing their description.
matched_golden_ids: Calling `i.content.scrub` assumes that `i.content` is always populated. However, many RSS feeds do not provide a `content` field, leading to a potential nil pointer exception when `i.content` is nil. A fallback to `description` should be implemented to prevent crashes.
adjudication_records.primary_judge_reasoning: The candidate issue identifies the exact same problem as the golden comment: RSS items without a content field will cause nil.scrub to raise an error, and the solution should involve falling back to description. Both comments point to the same bug at the same location (line 35 in poll_feed.rb), identifying the nil pointer issue when i.content is not populated and suggesting description as a fallback.

adjudication_records.issue_text: spec/controllers/embed_controller_spec.rb:43 — This test still requires a synchronous TopicRetriever call even though the controller now only enqueues a job, so the suite will fail.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the test in spec/controllers/embed_controller_spec.rb:43, it tests that when no previous embed is found, the controller enqueues a job. The test mocks TopicRetriever and expects it to be called with retrieve. However, looking at the controller code in app/controllers/embed_controller.rb:14, when topic_id is nil, it calls `Jobs.enqueue(:retrieve_topic, ...)` which enqueues a background job, not directly calling TopicRetriever. The test expects `TopicRetriever.expects(:new).returns(retriever)` and `retriever.expects(:retrieve)`, but the controller doesn't directly instantiate TopicRetriever - it enqueues a job that will later do that. This means the test expectations don't match the actual controller behavior, and the test would fail because TopicRetriever.new is never called directly by the controller.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/models/topic_embed.rb:64 — Protocol-relative URLs such as //cdn.example/x are incorrectly rewritten onto the article host, breaking imported links and images.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the code in app/models/topic_embed.rb lines 53-70, the absolutize_urls method checks if href/src start_with?('/') and then prepends the prefix. However, protocol-relative URLs like '//cdn.example/x' also start with '/', so they would be incorrectly rewritten to 'http://eviltrout.com//cdn.example/x' (after the sub(/^\/+/, '') removes leading slashes, it becomes 'http://eviltrout.com/cdn.example/x'). This is a real bug - protocol-relative URLs should be left alone or handled differently, but instead they get mangled into invalid URLs pointing to the wrong host.

adjudication_records.issue_text: lib/tasks/disqus.thor:148 — Replacing PostCreator with import_remote silently drops both the requested category and the exported thread creation timestamp.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the diff for lib/tasks/disqus.thor, the old code at line 144 used PostCreator.new with parameters including 'created_at: Date.parse(t[:created_at])' and 'category: category_id'. The new code at line 143 replaces this with 'TopicEmbed.import_remote(user, t[:link], title: t[:title])'. The import_remote method in topic_embed.rb only accepts 'opts[:title]' and passes it to TopicEmbed.import, which then uses PostCreator with 'title', 'raw', 'skip_validations', and 'cook_method' - but NOT 'created_at' or 'category'. Additionally, the '--category' option was removed from the method_options (line 117 removed). This means the thread creation timestamp (t[:created_at]) is indeed lost, and category support is removed. This is a real functional regression where imported Disqus threads will lose their original creation dates and category assignment capability.

adjudication_records.issue_text: db/migrate/20131219203905_add_cook_method_to_posts.rb:3 — Adding a NOT NULL column with a default rewrites and exclusively locks the potentially large posts table during deployment.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies that adding a NOT NULL column with a default value to the posts table in PostgreSQL (which Rails uses) will rewrite the entire table and hold an exclusive lock. For a large posts table, this can cause significant downtime during deployment. This is a real operational/deployment concern. The migration at db/migrate/20131219203905_add_cook_method_to_posts.rb does exactly this: `add_column :posts, :cook_method, :integer, default: 1, null: false`. This is a well-known PostgreSQL issue where adding a column with a default and NOT NULL constraint requires rewriting all existing rows.

adjudication_records.issue_text: db/migrate/20131217174004_create_topic_embeds.rb:3 — force: true can silently drop a preexisting topic_embeds table and all of its data when this migration runs.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the diff, db/migrate/20131217174004_create_topic_embeds.rb creates a new table with 'force: true'. This is a new migration file being added (the file didn't exist before). In Rails migrations, 'force: true' means it will drop the table if it already exists before creating it. However, this is a brand new migration for a brand new feature (topic embeds). The table topic_embeds wouldn't exist before this migration runs. While 'force: true' is generally considered bad practice in migrations because it could cause data loss if the migration is run multiple times or if the table somehow already exists, in this specific context of a new feature being added, the risk is minimal. That said, the finding is technically correct - using 'force: true' in a migration is a real issue because migrations should be idempotent and safe to run, and 'force: true' violates this principle by potentially dropping existing data without warning.

adjudication_records.issue_text: db/migrate/20131223171005_create_top_topics.rb:3 — Changing this existing migration to force: true leaves deployed databases unchanged while making reruns destructively drop top_topics.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows a change to an existing migration file db/migrate/20131223171005_create_top_topics.rb, changing 'create_table :top_topics do |t|' to 'create_table :top_topics, force: true do |t|'. This is a real problem because: 1) Modifying existing migrations that have already been run in production is dangerous - the change won't be applied to deployed databases since migrations only run once, 2) Adding 'force: true' means if this migration is ever re-run (e.g., in development or testing), it will DROP the existing top_topics table and recreate it, potentially losing data, 3) This creates inconsistency between environments where the migration was run before vs after this change. This is a legitimate concern about migration safety.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/models/topic_embed.rb:9 — TopicEmbed now mixes persistence, remote fetching, HTML rewriting, and post orchestration despite TopicRetriever introducing a separate retrieval service.

adjudication.rationale: The finding describes a design/architecture concern about TopicEmbed having multiple responsibilities (persistence, remote fetching, HTML rewriting, post orchestration). Looking at the diff, TopicEmbed does indeed contain: 1) import() for creating/updating posts, 2) import_remote() for fetching remote content, 3) absolutize_urls() for URL rewriting, 4) topic_id_for_embed() for lookups. While TopicRetriever exists as a separate class, it actually delegates back to TopicEmbed.import_remote(). However, this is a design/architecture opinion about code organization and separation of concerns - not a bug, security issue, or correctness problem. The code functions correctly as written. This is a style/design nit rather than a real defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/jobs/scheduled/poll_feed.rb:20 — PollFeed#feed_key and its Digest dependency are dead code because nothing invokes the method.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the diff for app/jobs/scheduled/poll_feed.rb, I can see the feed_key method is defined at lines 20-22 but is never called anywhere in the file or in any other file in this diff. The method creates a cache key using Digest::SHA1 but nothing uses this key. The poll_feed method doesn't use feed_key at all. This is indeed dead code - the method and its Digest dependency serve no purpose in the current implementation.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/jobs/regular/retrieve_topic.rb:1 — The new job loads email/sender even though it never references email delivery code.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at app/jobs/regular/retrieve_topic.rb, line 1 has `require_dependency 'email/sender'`. The job class RetrieveTopic only uses TopicRetriever to retrieve topics and doesn't use any email functionality. This is an unnecessary require that adds dead code/dependency. However, this is more of a code cleanliness/style issue rather than a bug, security issue, or correctness problem. The code will still function correctly with this unnecessary require - it just loads code that isn't used. This is a minor code quality issue, not a real defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/controllers/embed_controller.rb:15 — Every cache-miss request enqueues a job before throttling, so repeated iframe loads can flood Sidekiq even when retrieval work is suppressed.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the embed_controller.rb code at line 15, when topic_id is nil, it enqueues a job with `Jobs.enqueue(:retrieve_topic, ...)`. However, examining the TopicRetriever class in lib/topic_retriever.rb, the `retrieved_recently?` method implements throttling using Redis setnx with a 60-second expiry. This throttling happens inside the job's `perform_retrieve` method, not before the job is enqueued. So the finding is correct - every cache-miss request will enqueue a Sidekiq job, and only then does the throttling check occur inside the job execution. Multiple iframe loads could indeed flood the Sidekiq queue with jobs, even though most of those jobs will exit early due to the throttle check. The job enqueue itself is not throttled.

adjudication_records.issue_text: lib/topic_retriever.rb:41 — Every distinct missing embed synchronously reruns the entire configured feed import, multiplying remote parsing and per-item database work by cache misses.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at lib/topic_retriever.rb:41, the perform_retrieve method checks if feed_polling_enabled? and if so, calls Jobs::PollFeed.new.execute({}). This executes the entire feed polling job synchronously. Looking at app/jobs/scheduled/poll_feed.rb, the poll_feed method fetches the RSS feed URL, parses it with SimpleRSS, and iterates through all items calling TopicEmbed.import for each. This means every time a user requests an embed URL that doesn't exist yet, if feed polling is enabled, the entire RSS feed is re-fetched and re-processed synchronously. This is indeed a real performance/scalability issue - multiple concurrent requests for different missing embed URLs would each trigger full feed imports, causing redundant remote fetches and database operations.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/models/topic_embed.rb:48 — The remote article body is read fully without a size bound before parsing, allowing a large response to exhaust worker memory.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at app/models/topic_embed.rb:48, the code is `doc = Readability::Document.new(open(url).read, ...)`. The `open(url).read` call fetches the entire remote content into memory without any size limit. If a malicious or misconfigured remote server returns an extremely large response, this could exhaust worker memory. This is a real security/resource exhaustion concern - the code does indeed read the full response body without bounds before parsing.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/jobs/scheduled/poll_feed.rb:29 — Feed polling downloads and materializes the complete feed and then processes every item without any response-size or item-count bound.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the poll_feed.rb code at line 29, the feed polling uses SimpleRSS.parse with open(SiteSetting.feed_polling_url) and then iterates through rss.items.each. The finding claims there's no response-size or item-count bound. This is accurate - the code downloads the entire feed without any size limit on the HTTP response, and processes all items in the feed without any limit on how many items to process. However, this is a scheduled background job (Jobs::Scheduled) that runs hourly, and RSS feeds are typically small. While technically true that there's no explicit bound, this is more of a theoretical concern for a background job processing RSS feeds. The code does have implicit bounds (RSS feeds are typically small, and the job runs periodically). This is more of a defensive programming suggestion than a clear defect - RSS feeds are designed to be small, and this is a common pattern for feed polling.

adjudication_records.issue_text: lib/topic_retriever.rb:27 — The throttle uses separate SETNX and EXPIRE calls, so a worker interruption between them leaves a permanent key that suppresses retrieval forever.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at lib/topic_retriever.rb lines 24-30, the code uses `$redis.setnx(retrieved_key, "1")` followed by `$redis.expire(retrieved_key, 60)` as separate calls. If the process crashes or is interrupted between these two calls, the key will be set without an expiration, causing it to persist indefinitely. This would permanently block retrieval for that embed_url. This is a real race condition bug - the atomic alternative would be to use `$redis.set(retrieved_key, "1", ex: 60, nx: true)` or similar atomic operation.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/jobs/scheduled/poll_feed.rb:12 — Disabling Sidekiq retries means a transient feed download or parse failure is not retried until the next hourly poll.

adjudication.rationale: The finding points to `sidekiq_options retry: false` on line 12 of poll_feed.rb. This is a valid observation - the code explicitly disables Sidekiq's automatic retry mechanism. However, this is a deliberate design choice, not a bug. The job runs hourly via `recurrence { hourly }`, so if a feed poll fails, it will naturally be retried in the next hourly run. Disabling retries for scheduled jobs that run frequently is a common and reasonable pattern to avoid queue buildup from repeated failures. The code is working as intended - it's a design decision rather than a defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/jobs/scheduled/poll_feed.rb:31 — A single malformed feed item aborts the entire batch without per-item isolation, preventing all later valid items from being imported.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the poll_feed.rb code, the `poll_feed` method iterates over `rss.items.each do |i|` and processes each item by calling `TopicEmbed.import(user, url, i.title, content)`. If any item in the loop throws an exception (e.g., due to malformed content, nil values, or encoding issues), the entire loop would abort and subsequent items would not be processed. There's no try/catch or error handling around individual item processing. The code does call `i.content.scrub` which could fail if `i.content` is nil, and there's no validation that required fields exist before processing. This is a real robustness issue where one bad feed item can prevent all subsequent items from being imported.

adjudication_records.issue_text: lib/topic_retriever.rb:50 — A missing embed user is silently treated as success, leaving the loading iframe to enqueue retrieval jobs forever without exposing a terminal configuration error.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at lib/topic_retriever.rb:50, the fetch_http method returns early if user is blank without any logging or error indication. When this happens, the TopicEmbed is never created, so TopicEmbed.where(embed_url: @embed_url).exists? will continue to return false. In embed_controller.rb, when topic_id is nil, it enqueues a RetrieveTopic job and renders 'loading'. The loading.html.erb has a 30-second auto-refresh. If embed_by_username is misconfigured (blank or invalid), each page refresh will enqueue another job, and fetch_http will silently return without creating the embed, causing an infinite loop of job enqueuing and page refreshes. This is a real configuration error that fails silently.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/models/topic_embed.rb:22 — Imported feed HTML bypasses the cooking sanitizer and is stored verbatim, allowing a malicious feed item to execute persistent script in topic and embed views.
matched_golden_ids: The TopicEmbed.import method is susceptible to a NoMethodError if the contents parameter is nil when attempting to append a string, and an XSS vulnerability due to unescaped url interpolation in the generated HTML.
adjudication_records.primary_judge_reasoning: The golden comment identifies two issues: 1) a NoMethodError if contents is nil, and 2) an XSS vulnerability due to unescaped url interpolation in generated HTML. The candidate issue identifies an XSS/script injection vulnerability where imported feed HTML bypasses sanitization. Both identify XSS vulnerabilities in the TopicEmbed.import method related to unsanitized content, though the golden comment specifically mentions 'unescaped url interpolation' while the candidate mentions 'feed HTML bypasses cooking sanitizer'. These are related XSS concerns in the same method, though the candidate doesn't mention the NoMethodError issue. The candidate partially matches - it identifies the XSS vulnerability aspect but misses the nil contents issue.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/models/topic_embed.rb:48 — The fetch follows redirects after validating only the initial hostname, allowing an allowed-host redirect to drive server-side requests into private network services.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at app/models/topic_embed.rb:48, the code uses `open(url).read` from the 'open-uri' library to fetch remote content. The validation at line 11 only checks if the URL starts with 'http://' or 'https://' using a regex. There's no validation that the hostname is in an allowed list before fetching. The `embeddable_host` setting is checked in `topic_retriever.rb` for the embed URL, but in `import_remote` method, any URL can be passed and fetched. If an attacker controls a page on the allowed embeddable_host that redirects to an internal service (like http://169.254.169.254 for cloud metadata), the initial URL validation passes but the redirect could reach internal services. However, looking more carefully, the `import_remote` is called from `topic_retriever.rb` which does validate the host matches `embeddable_host` before calling `fetch_http`. The RSS feed polling in `poll_feed.rb` also fetches from a configured URL. The SSRF concern is valid - if an allowed host redirects to internal services, open-uri will follow those redirects. This is a real security concern as open-uri follows redirects by default.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/controllers/embed_controller.rb:15 — This public action authenticates only with a forgeable Referer and enqueues before throttling, so repeated requests can flood the job queue and trigger attacker-chosen imports.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the embed_controller.rb code: The `best` action checks embeddable_host and validates that request.referer host matches SiteSetting.embeddable_host in `ensure_embeddable`. The Referer header is indeed forgeable by attackers. When no topic_id is found, it enqueues a job via `Jobs.enqueue(:retrieve_topic, ...)` BEFORE any throttling occurs in the controller itself. The throttling logic exists in TopicRetriever (retrieved_recently? method using Redis setnx with 60 second expiry), but this happens INSIDE the job execution, not before enqueueing. This means an attacker can forge the Referer header and repeatedly hit the endpoint to flood the job queue with retrieve_topic jobs. While each job will be throttled internally, the queue itself can be flooded. Additionally, the Referer-based authentication is weak security. This is a real concern - the authentication relies on a forgeable header and jobs are enqueued before rate limiting.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/assets/javascripts/embed.js:17 — Substring-based origin validation accepts shorter attacker-controlled origins contained in discourseUrl, allowing cross-origin messages to manipulate the embed frame height.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the code in app/assets/javascripts/embed.js line 16-17: `if (discourseUrl.indexOf(e.origin) === -1) { return; }`. This checks if e.origin is found anywhere within discourseUrl. The problem is that indexOf returns -1 only if the substring is NOT found. So if e.origin IS found within discourseUrl, indexOf returns >= 0, and the check passes. However, the vulnerability claim is about 'shorter attacker-controlled origins contained in discourseUrl'. For example, if discourseUrl is 'https://discourse.example.com', an attacker origin like 'example.com' would pass this check because 'example.com' is contained within the URL string. This is a real security issue - the validation should check if discourseUrl starts with e.origin or use proper URL parsing, not substring matching. An attacker could register a domain that is a substring of the legitimate discourse URL and send malicious postMessage events.

adjudication_records.issue_text: spec/controllers/embed_controller_spec.rb:43 — The no-embed example still expects a synchronous TopicRetriever call even though the controller now enqueues a job, so this spec fails instead of verifying the queue contract.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the diff, the embed_controller.rb shows that when no topic_id is found, it calls `Jobs.enqueue(:retrieve_topic, ...)` to enqueue a background job. However, the test in spec/controllers/embed_controller_spec.rb at line 43 sets up expectations like `TopicRetriever.expects(:new).returns(retriever)` and `retriever.expects(:retrieve)`, expecting synchronous TopicRetriever calls. But the controller actually enqueues a job via `Jobs.enqueue(:retrieve_topic, ...)`, not calling TopicRetriever directly. The TopicRetriever is called inside the job (lib/jobs/regular/retrieve_topic.rb), not in the controller. So the test expectations don't match the actual controller behavior - the test expects direct TopicRetriever instantiation but the controller enqueues a job instead. This would cause the test to fail.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/jobs/scheduled/poll_feed.rb:36 — PollFeed tests only mock delegation and never parse a feed, leaving ordinary RSS items without content to crash on nil.scrub.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the diff, in app/jobs/scheduled/poll_feed.rb line 36, the code does `content = CGI.unescapeHTML(i.content.scrub)`. If an RSS item doesn't have a 'content' field (i.content returns nil), calling .scrub on nil would raise a NoMethodError. The finding correctly identifies that the test in spec/jobs/poll_feed_spec.rb only mocks the poll_feed method call and never actually tests parsing real RSS data, so this nil case wouldn't be caught. This is a real bug - RSS feeds commonly have items without content fields (they might only have description, summary, or other fields), and the code doesn't handle this case.

adjudication_records.issue_text: spec/models/topic_embed_spec.rb:18 — The malformed-URL test only covers text rejected by the regex, so scheme-only values such as http:// remain accepted and can be imported.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the TopicEmbed.import method in app/models/topic_embed.rb, line 11 shows: `return unless url =~ /^https?\:\/\//`. This regex checks that the URL starts with 'http://' or 'https://'. The test in spec/models/topic_embed_spec.rb:18 uses 'invalid url' which doesn't match this pattern. The finding claims that 'http://' alone would pass the regex - let's verify: 'http://' matches `^https?\:\/\/` because it starts with 'http://'. So technically 'http://' would pass the regex check. However, this would then fail when trying to create a URI from it or when the content is processed. The finding is technically correct that the regex would accept 'http://' as valid, but this is a minor edge case that would likely fail downstream. The test does cover the intended case of rejecting obviously malformed URLs. This is more of a test coverage suggestion than a real bug in the production code.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/assets/javascripts/embed.js:17 — No JavaScript test covers message-origin validation, leaving prefix origins accepted by the substring check and able to resize the iframe.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the code in embed.js line 17: `if (discourseUrl.indexOf(e.origin) === -1) { return; }`. This check uses indexOf which means if discourseUrl is 'http://example.com', an origin like 'http://example.com.evil.com' would pass the check (indexOf would return 0, not -1). This is a real security issue - the origin validation is flawed because it uses substring matching instead of exact matching. An attacker could set up a domain that contains the legitimate discourseUrl as a prefix and send malicious resize messages to manipulate the iframe height. The finding correctly identifies this as a security vulnerability in the message-origin validation.
